# FDG7018

> DO throw the most specific (the most derived) exception that makes sense.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 7.2 Choosing the Right Type of Exception to Throw.

## How it is checked

- Check: sdk (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: CA2201
- Automatic fix: no
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test warning
- Status: verified

CA2201 reports creating System.Exception, System.SystemException and System.ApplicationException, which are never the most specific exception (the Richter annotation). Whether another type is the most derived one that makes sense, such as ArgumentNullException rather than ArgumentException, is not checked, so coverage is partial. CA2201's reports of runtime-reserved types belong to FDG7045 to FDG7049. CA2201 has no code fix.

## From the book

For example, throw `ArgumentNullException` and not its base type, `ArgumentException`, if a null argument is passed.

> **Jeffrey Richter:** Throwing `System.Exception`, the base class of all CLS-compliant exceptions, is always the wrong thing to do.

> **Brent Rector:** As described in more detail later, catching `System.Exception` is nearly always the wrong thing to do as well.

Now that you have chosen the correct exception type, you can focus on ensuring that the error message your exception delivers says what you need it to say.
